newsitem.title: USA: UAW workers poised to strike GM pickup truck plant.
newsitem.headline: UAW workers poised to strike GM pickup truck plant.

text.p: Nearly 5,500 hourly workers were poised to strike a General Motors Corp. pickup truck plant on Tuesday night in a dispute over jobs and the use of outside suppliers, adding to the labor woes at the world's largest automaker.

Members of United Auto Worker Local 594 in Pontiac, Mich., were drawing up picket signs and preparing to walk off the job when a strike deadline expires at 11:59 p.m. Tuesday, said Jim Abare, an official at the union local.
"It's looking that way," said Abare, referring to the possibility of a walkout.
GM spokesman Dan Flores said the two sides resumed talks for a new contract Tuesday morning after bargaining for more than 14 hours on Monday.
"We're hopeful we can reach a tentative settlement without a work stoppage," he said.
Since January, GM has been hit with three strikes by union locals demanding the automaker address health and safety issues and add more workers.

GM's national contract with the UAW, signed last November, allows it to reduce its U.S. hourly workforce of 215,000 by about 30,000 over the three-year pact. GM still has to reach tentative agreements with 25 percent of its 105 UAW locals, far behind the other members of the U.S. Big Three.

About 4,100 UAW members work on the assembly line at GM's Pontiac East truck assembly plant. Another 1,300 union members work in engineering, product development and simulated manufacturing facilities associated with GM's Truck Product Center, located near the plant.

Also affected by the walkout would be 450 members of Local 594 who work at a Lear Corp. seating plant in nearby Rochester Hills, Mich. The workers were hired two years ago as part of an agreement to settle a strike at the Pontiac plant. A Lear representative could not be reached for comment.
The GM facility makes the popular and high-profit full-size regular cab and extended cab GMC Sierra and Chevrolet C/K pickup trucks. It also makes chassis cab trucks.
The plant produced 72,000 vehicles in the first three months of this year, equal to a weekly output of about 6,000 vehicles.

Abare at Local 594 would not say specifically what the union was demanding, although he said manpower disputes were the major concerns. The union also wants GM to resolve occupational health issues and live up to promises it made to settle the strike in 1995, he said.
"It was signed, sealed, but never delivered," Abare said of the 1995 settlement.

GM is still battling a strike at its Oklahoma City, Okla., car plant by 3,500 members of UAW Local 1999 that started April 4. The plant makes the Chevrolet Malibu and Oldsmobile Cutlass, two mid-size sedans crucial to GM's U.S. sales strategy.
GM spokesman Vince Muniga said Tuesday talks continue in Oklahoma City, with a number of issues being resolved within the last few days.

Meanwhile, Chrysler Corp. and the UAW are trying to settle an engine plant strike, that stretched into its 13th day Tuesday. More than 22,000 hourly workers at Chrysler plants in North America have been idled as a result of the strike.
